lines.text: A wallet costs nothing to make.
One person can cast five thousand votes.
The usual fix? Hand over your identity.
Judges takes a proof instead.
Your passkey stays on your device.
A zero-knowledge proof says you're a member, not which one.
Monad checks it and spends a nullifier.
One credential, one action.
Four steps. Nothing else disclosed.
That's the idea. Here it is, running on Monad testnet.
This verdict is read from a real transaction.
You register once: a passkey prompt, then one wallet signature.
First app: a faucet that pays once per credential. I connect a wallet.
I ask to claim, and the wallet signs one message. That signature becomes my secret. It never leaves this browser.
The proof is built right here. No server learns who I am.
Then it goes to Monad. The contract checks the proof and marks my nullifier as spent.
Accepted.
Now the same credential tries again. Same secret, same app, same nullifier.
Rejected. And nothing was even sent.
Second app: a DAO. Same identity, different app, so a fresh nullifier.

lines.text: One credential, one vote. The proof is bound to my choice, so nobody can copy it and flip it.
Counted.
A second vote? Rejected.
Third: a registry for AI agents. An agent is recorded only when a verified credential stands behind it. No identity is stored.
For a developer, it's two calls: prove, then verify.
The hard choice was cost. Checking a passkey directly on chain is about thirteen times cheaper. But your public key would follow you into every app.
So Judges pays for the proof: about 1.1 million gas on Monad.
What it does not prove is one person, one credential. Someone can still register twice. Judges says so in its own dissent.
What it does prove: a user-verified passkey stood behind this wallet. Nothing else disclosed.
Judges. Open source, and live on Monad testnet.
